title: 75 Assessment of the Steer-A-Year Program at Montana State University
content:
Abstract
Objective: This study aimed to assess the educational, operational, and stakeholder impacts of the Montana State University (MSU) Steer-A-Year (SAY) program, which integrates experiential learning into beef cattle production education. The program’s interdisciplinary nature provides students, donors, and industry supporters with practical, real-world insights into livestock management and agricultural systems. This research sought to evaluate these impacts and identify areas for improvement to enhance program sustainability and stakeholder engagement. Methods: A qualitative research approach was employed, utilizing focus groups with three stakeholder groups: students, donors, and industry supporters. Participants were selected based on their involvement in the program. Data collection included structured discussions, field notes, and audio recordings, enabling an in-depth exploration of stakeholder experiences. Thematic analysis was conducted to identify recurring patterns, challenges, and successes. Ethical clearance was obtained through the Institutional Review Board (IRB) at MSU, ensuring the research adhered to ethical standards for human subject participation. Results: Students emphasized the program’s hands-on learning opportunities, which allowed them to apply theoretical concepts to real-world scenarios. Through activities such as feedlot management, carcass evaluation, and donor engagement, participants reported improved technical skills, critical thinking, and professional confidence. Many credited the program with influencing their career paths and broadening their understanding of the beef production cycle. Donors highlighted the value of receiving detailed performance data on their steers, which informed breeding and feeding strategies. However, logistical challenges, including variability in donated livestock and coordination difficulties, were noted as areas requiring improvement. Industry supporters praised the interdisciplinary collaboration, particularly the integration of beef products into MSU culinary services, which connected production to consumer experiences. This partnership not only provided students with exposure to the complete production chain but also fostered public awareness of sustainable agriculture. Despite its successes, stakeholders identified infrastructure limitations, such as outdated facilities and constrained resources, as barriers to the program’s growth and efficiency. Conclusion: The MSU Steer-A-Year program exemplifies the transformative potential of experiential learning in agricultural education. By bridging theoretical knowledge and practical application, it equips students with valuable skills and fosters meaningful connections between academia and industry. Addressing identified challenges: including infrastructure upgrades, standardized operational practices, and expanded stakeholder engagement, will enhance the program’s sustainability and long-term impact. These findings underscore the importance of experiential learning frameworks in preparing students for the complexities of modern agriculture, while simultaneously advancing industry practices and strengthening community ties. The SAY program serves as a replicable model for integrating education, research, and outreach to meet the evolving needs of the agricultural sector.
